motion: Can one reasonably believe the Bible is revealed by God despite its violent passages?

bridges.description: Show that morally troubling violent passages can be acknowledged and interpreted within a reasonable belief that the Bible mediates divine revelation.
Ground interpretation of diverse biblical genres in the disclosed center of Jesus and the norm of increasing love of God and neighbor.
Defend reasonable religious belief without certainty by challenging an overly restrictive public-verification requirement.
Argue that biblical depictions of divine violence and judgment conflict with a morally perfect revealer and make belief in divine revelation unreasonable.
Require religious claims to be supported by objectively verifiable facts that indicate or uniquely fit the proposed explanation.
Argue that factual failures and divergent theological readings undermine treating the Bible as a clear, reliable revelation.

sections.title: Moral standards and biblical violence
sections.rationale: The motion directly turns on whether depictions of stoning, genocide, and divine commands can be reconciled with objective moral judgment and a perfect revealer.

sections.title: Scripture, genre, and revelatory reading
sections.rationale: A central dispute concerns whether the Bible should be read as a flat factual record or as a diverse collection interpreted through genre and a Christian theological center.

sections.title: Jesus's authority and historical reading
sections.rationale: The speakers separately test the proposed Jesus-centered reading through alleged first-century error and Jesus's use of disputed biblical narratives.

sections.title: Judgment, salvation, and divine character
sections.rationale: The speakers treat judgment and hell as further tests of whether the biblical God is morally credible and whether competing readings preserve a coherent divine character.

sections.title: Evidential standards and error correction
sections.rationale: The debate over objective verification, private experience, fallibility, and proportional evidence defines what each side counts as accountable belief.

sections.title: Skepticism and fallibilist reasonableness
sections.rationale: The later exchange asks whether skeptical possibilities defeat knowledge and whether reasonable belief can remain fallible while responsive to defeaters.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Both naturalists and Christian theists must test their broader views against apparent objective moral facts.
moves.warrant: People commonly recognize acts such as hanging a child as objectively evil, while naturalism and Christianity each face different tensions in accommodating such judgments.
moves.inference: Biblical violence is a real internal challenge for Christianity, but encountering that challenge calls for rational revision or interpretation rather than immediate rejection of the whole worldview.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is the complete opening comparison from the objective-evil example through Rauser's explicit statement of the Christian's biblical-violence problem and shared accommodation burden.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: there is such a thing as objective good
we all with our worldviews we have to wrestle with moral content
moves.attributionRationale: Rauser delivers an uninterrupted opening explanation, with the moderator only briefly urging a return to the topic.
moves.importanceRationale: It frames Rauser's motion-level route by conceding the moral problem and defining how reasonable belief should respond to it.

burdenContact.rationale: It treats violent biblical material as evidence requiring reconciliation within, or revision of, Christian belief.

moves.speaker: Aron Ra
moves.claim: A command attributed to God does not by itself establish an objective moral standard.
moves.warrant: If morality is fixed only by what a deity says, it rests on the deity's or an alleged representative's subjective assertion without an independent reason.
moves.inference: Biblical divine commands can still be judged evil by shared moral criteria rather than being insulated from criticism by their claimed source.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage begins with Aron's proposed criterion for objective evil and ends after his reason that divine say-so is not an explanation.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: Does it fit the definition of evil
because I said so is not an explanation
moves.attributionRationale: The brief assent at event 468 is Rauser; the selected claim and quoted language are Aron's continuous surrounding turn.
moves.importanceRationale: This directly contests whether divine authorship could neutralize the moral force of violent passages.

burdenContact.rationale: It preserves external moral assessment of purported divine violence.

responseComponents.description: Accepts the need to accommodate moral facts but denies that theism secures objectivity merely by invoking God's command.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Moral reasoning need not begin with a fully derived formal definition because some moral beliefs function as basic starting points.
moves.warrant: Demanding a further reason for every claim creates an infinite regress, while people can build moral understanding by directly recognizing paradigm cases of evil and good.
moves.inference: Objective moral criticism of biblical violence can be retained without requiring an independently proved abstract definition before interpretation begins.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This complete response runs from the regress objection through the explanation of properly basic beliefs and ostensive moral recognition.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: That would immediately set you off on an infinite regress
we point at things in the world
moves.attributionRationale: Rauser speaks continuously and explicitly answers Aron's demand for reasons and definitions.
moves.importanceRationale: It supports the moral framework Rauser uses to reject atrocity while maintaining a revelatory reading.

burdenContact.rationale: It supplies the moral epistemology that allows him to treat some violent acts as genuinely wrong while reconsidering the text's interpretation.

responseComponents.description: Answers the demand for a reason behind moral judgments by locating some judgments among properly basic starting points rather than bare divine say-so.

moves.speaker: Aron Ra
moves.claim: Unnecessary harm, pain, suffering, or death provides a workable starting criterion for moral wrongness.
moves.warrant: The criterion captures ordinary moral judgment while allowing further nuance for hard allocation cases.
moves.inference: Biblical conduct can be tested against a comprehensible harm standard instead of being excused by theological authority.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains Aron's full proposed rule, his qualification about hard cases, and his application to conflicting claims about what God says.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: it is immoral or wrong to unnecessarily
cause pain or suffering or death
moves.attributionRationale: This is Aron's uninterrupted response until Rauser begins at event 575.
moves.importanceRationale: It states the substantive moral criterion behind Aron's objections to violent commands.

burdenContact.rationale: It provides the standard by which biblical violence is alleged to conflict with moral perfection.

responseComponents.description: Offers a verbalized moral rule in place of relying only on pointed paradigm cases.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Christians must not minimize the cruelty of biblical stoning and genocide narratives and may need to reinterpret those texts.
moves.warrant: Stoning is inhumane, genocide resembles atrocities such as Rwanda, and rationales rejected elsewhere cannot become legitimate merely because a biblical text attributes them to God.
moves.inference: A morally serious Christian can preserve the claim that God is perfect only by refusing atrocity-affirming readings and using the tradition's resources for alternative interpretation.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins when Rauser introduces biblical stoning and retains the complete linked stoning, genocide, Rwanda, perfect-being, and reinterpretation argument through his conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: we need to have a thick narrative description
you can't then attribute to God
moves.attributionRationale: Rauser owns the sustained case; Aron's short additions at 744–752 and challenge at 776–784 are not used as Rauser's quoted support.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Rauser's fullest direct treatment of the violent passages named by the motion.

burdenContact.rationale: It explains why the violent material must be confronted and why reinterpretation is available to belief in a morally perfect revealer.

moves.speaker: Aron Ra
moves.claim: If God is perfect, the Bible's portrayal of violent and misleading conduct points to a different agent or to a false account.
moves.warrant: The text presents conduct Aron regards as immoral, while a perfect being would not exhibit those defects.
moves.inference: Even granting that a perfect God exists, the Bible can fail as revelation because its depicted character does not match that God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This compact autobiographical argument states the perfect-God premise, the mismatch, and the resulting conclusion about the Bible.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: if God is a perfect person
If there is a God, the Bible's still wrong
moves.attributionRationale: Aron speaks continuously from his childhood test through the stated conclusion.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly converts the violence-and-character objection into a conclusion about revelation rather than God's existence.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that moral perfection and the Bible's portrait cannot jointly support divine revelation.

responseComponents.description: Presses the conceded perfect-being standard toward rejecting the Bible rather than repairing it through interpretation.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: The Bible should be read as a diverse ancient anthology rather than through one uniform literal method.
moves.warrant: Its texts arise from different genres, languages, cultures, and historical settings, much as an anthology contains writings that require distinct reading practices.
moves.inference: Difficult violent or historically framed passages cannot establish the unreasonableness of revelation until their particular literary setting is considered.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage contains the full anthology analogy and its conclusion about cultural, linguistic, and interpretive distance.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the Bible is a complicated book
we have to appreciate the distance
moves.attributionRationale: Rauser speaks without a substantive handoff throughout the analogy.
moves.importanceRationale: Genre-sensitive interpretation is a central bridge in Rauser's answer to violent texts.

burdenContact.rationale: It establishes the need for differentiated reading before the theological criterion is applied.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the move from troubling portrayals to a wholesale verdict by insisting that the collected texts require genre-sensitive interpretation.

moves.speaker: Aron Ra
moves.claim: The Bible is best treated as culturally developed folklore rather than as privileged revelation.
moves.warrant: It contains differing legal presentations, draws on earlier traditions, and reflects changing audiences and political purposes.
moves.inference: A text assembled through ordinary cultural processes lacks a demonstrated basis for special revelatory authority.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Aron's complete initial folklore argument, including differing legal presentations, claimed reuse of earlier traditions, and his conclusion that the collection does not warrant special reverence.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: it's folklore and that's all it can be
I can't give it any more reverence than that
moves.attributionRationale: Aron owns the continuous turn; the quoted phrases are his words and do not depend on the later clarification exchange.
moves.importanceRationale: It gives Aron's alternative account of what kind of book the Bible is.

burdenContact.rationale: It attributes the Bible's diversity to cultural composition rather than divine disclosure.

responseComponents.description: Accepts diversity but argues that it supports a folklore classification rather than revelatory status.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Calling the whole Bible folklore repeats the same flattening error as reading the whole collection like a newspaper.
moves.warrant: The collection includes wisdom, biography, letters, apocalypse, creation narrative, and other genres with distinct purposes and conventions.
moves.inference: The revelatory claim must be assessed through the actual kinds of text present, not a single dismissive classification.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This response includes Rauser's clarification of two senses of folklore and his complete list-based argument for distinct genres.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: that's another single categorization
we have to be careful about any single brush
moves.attributionRationale: The exchange includes Aron's clarification at 952–958; Rauser's surrounding reply and quoted text are clearly separated.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly protects the genre premise from Aron's alternative global label.

burdenContact.rationale: It supports differentiated interpretation as a condition for judging revelation.

responseComponents.description: Argues that the folklore label fails to preserve the collection's materially different literary forms.

moves.speaker: Aron Ra
moves.claim: The Bible's religious development is culturally explicable and does not establish factual accuracy.
moves.warrant: Aron compares Christian reuse of Hebrew and other religious elements with later Islamic reuse and reinterpretation of earlier traditions.
moves.inference: Intertextual development and selective appropriation are insufficient grounds for treating the resulting collection as revealed truth.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is the complete cultural-development reply from Aron's acceptance of the collection description through his explicit accuracy conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: it's a cultural collective
it's not any of it factually accurate
moves.attributionRationale: Aron speaks continuously in this span.
moves.importanceRationale: It connects the genre discussion to the epistemic question of revelatory truth.

burdenContact.rationale: It offers ordinary cultural transmission as a rival explanation for the collection's form.

responseComponents.description: Concedes internal variety while denying that variety supplies factual or divine authority.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: For Christian reading, Jesus and the increase of love for God and neighbor provide the governing interpretive center.
moves.warrant: Rauser links 2 Timothy's purpose for scripture, Augustine's rule of love, and Jesus's extension of neighbor-love to outsiders and enemies.
moves.inference: Readings that use violent passages to dehumanize or harm others misread the Bible's Christian purpose, while nonviolent reinterpretation remains available.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The full span is needed to preserve the linked scriptural, Augustinian, and Jesus-centered grounds for the interpretive criterion and its practical conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the center is is Jesus
Are you increasing in your love of God and of other people
moves.attributionRationale: Rauser's main exposition is continuous, with Aron's brief citation query at 1069–1079 answered inside the same argument.
moves.importanceRationale: This is the positive hermeneutic by which Rauser proposes to read violent passages as revelation.

burdenContact.rationale: It supplies the central theological rule for evaluating and appropriating diverse biblical texts.

moves.speaker: Aron Ra
moves.claim: Known failures of literal biblical narratives undermine trust in the Bible as a reliable source.
moves.warrant: Aron cites Adam and Eve, a global flood, Babel, the Exodus, and Moses as narratives that scientific or scholarly inquiry does not support in their ordinary historical form.
moves.inference: A book wrong about many foundational claims does not merit special confidence merely because a theological reading extracts other meanings.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage begins with Aron's truth-centered objection to the love criterion and ends with his explicit trust conclusion after the historical examples.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: shouldn't understanding truth
why would we put such trust into a book
moves.attributionRationale: Aron speaks continuously until Rauser begins his response.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly challenges the reasonableness of privileging the Bible when key narratives are disputed as history.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that flexible interpretation does not repair the underlying reliability problem.

responseComponents.description: Challenges love as the primary reading goal by insisting that truth and historical reliability remain prior tests.

moves.speaker: Aron Ra
moves.claim: Jesus's reported medical assumptions are evidence against treating him as an authoritative source of transcendent wisdom.
moves.warrant: Aron argues that Jesus opposed purity practices on grounds that ignore poisons and pathogens and interpreted disease through demons.
moves.inference: A figure who shares first-century medical errors does not provide an adequate center for treating the Bible as divine revelation.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins with Aron's direct reply to living like Jesus and includes the complete linked examples about ingestion, handwashing, pathogens, and demons through his authority conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: didn't understand poisons or nutrients or drugs
he thinks that diseases are caused by demons
moves.attributionRationale: Aron speaks continuously throughout this challenge.
moves.importanceRationale: It is a distinct objection to the reliability of Rauser's proposed Jesus-centered interpretive norm.

burdenContact.rationale: It challenges the authority of the figure used to organize the revelatory reading.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Even if Jesus held one mistaken historical medical belief, that would not show that he was wholly unreliable or devoid of wisdom.
moves.warrant: Earlier scientists accepted a geocentric model because it reflected the best understanding available in their setting, yet that error does not make all of their work worthless.
moves.inference: A claimed first-century limitation cannot by itself defeat Jesus's broader moral or revelatory authority.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span starts with Rauser granting Aron's premise for argument and contains the complete Ptolemaic-science analogy and sociohistorical conclusion; Aron's interruptions asserting that diseases are not caused by demons and asking what Jesus was right about are not used as Rauser evidence.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: it doesn't follow that a person who was wrong on a particular issue
the best knowledge and understanding at that time
moves.attributionRationale: Rauser owns the reply around two clearly identifiable Aron interruptions at events 1245–1246 and 1255.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly answers the inference from a particular medical error to wholesale rejection of Jesus's authority.

burdenContact.rationale: It defends the viability of using Jesus as an interpretive center despite a proposed historical limitation.

responseComponents.description: Denies that one alleged medical error establishes global unreliability or lack of wisdom.

moves.speaker: Aron Ra
moves.claim: Christian judgment appears to make eternal outcome depend on belief rather than morally relevant conduct.
moves.warrant: Aron argues that belief grants forgiveness while disbelief remains unforgiven regardless of whether a person is otherwise good or bad.
moves.inference: A revelation that grounds ultimate judgment in assent rather than conduct portrays an unjust system and weakens its moral credibility.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This span contains Aron's setup, reformulation, and complete belief-versus-action objection before Rauser answers.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: entirely entirely on what you do or don't believe
the only sin that will not be forgiven
moves.attributionRationale: Aron's position is continuous apart from Rauser's short prompt to quote the basis.
moves.importanceRationale: It is Aron's main moral objection to biblical judgment beyond the violence narratives.

burdenContact.rationale: It broadens the claimed conflict between the biblical God and moral perfection to eternal judgment.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Jesus's sheep-and-goats parable depicts judgment in terms of how people treat others, not mere professed belief.
moves.warrant: The separation turns on feeding, clothing, and visiting people in need, while some who assume themselves righteous are rejected.
moves.inference: The biblical account includes an action-centered and self-critical model of judgment that resists Aron's belief-only reconstruction.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage gives the full parable-based answer from introduction through its action-centered conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: It is how they responded to others
all about action, what you do
moves.attributionRationale: Rauser speaks continuously through the complete parable explanation.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly answers the belief-only charge with a central counterexample from Jesus.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that the revealed moral framework is less arbitrary than the con account alleges.

responseComponents.description: Counters the assertion that judgment is solely about belief with a conduct-based biblical passage.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: The unforgivable-sin warning concerns a willful refusal to recognize good or truth presented directly, not innocent absence of belief.
moves.warrant: In the narrative, opponents attribute an apparent healing to the devil rather than acknowledge the sign before them.
moves.inference: The warning targets resistant moral agency, so it does not establish that sincere evidential doubt alone is eternally punished.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins after Aron's answer naming the Holy Spirit and contains Rauser's complete narrative-context explanation through its consequence.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: people who refuse to submit and recognize truth
right in front of them
moves.attributionRationale: Rauser speaks continuously through the contextual explanation.
moves.importanceRationale: This is the exact target of Aron's ensuing submission and coercion objection.

burdenContact.rationale: It defends the moral scope of a difficult judgment passage.

responseComponents.description: Narrows the alleged belief-only rule to willful rejection of recognized truth in the narrative context.

moves.speaker: Aron Ra
moves.claim: A demand to submit to religious truth under irreversible eternal consequences is coercive and unjust.
moves.warrant: Finite people have limited evidence and opportunity, while the proposed judgment offers no rehabilitation and may inherit blame from agents without moral knowledge.
moves.inference: The judgment narrative does not become morally credible by describing rejection as willful refusal to submit.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins with Aron's own interruption, preserves his complete response to the 'refuse to submit and recognize truth' formulation, and ends with his conclusion about Christianity's lack of a redeeming feature.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: It's about control. It's about manipulation of the masses
allow anybody a means of u rehabilitation
moves.attributionRationale: Aron speaks continuously from his request to consider the submission language through the mute interruption.
moves.importanceRationale: It targets the moral meaning of the pro explanation rather than merely repeating the belief-only objection.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that the proposed divine judgment remains incompatible with a morally trustworthy revealer.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the characterization of resistant nonbelief as refusal to submit and argues that finite evidence plus irreversible consequences makes the demand coercive.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Judgment accounts for the information available to each person, and damnation is chosen alienation rather than punishment for missing a proposition.
moves.warrant: Rauser appeals to people being judged by the moral light they possess and interprets hostile refusal of reconciliation as self-exclusion that God does not forcefully override.
moves.inference: Sincere lack of access or mistaken belief is not itself the basis of condemnation, reducing the alleged arbitrariness and coercion.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains the complete two-part answer: differential access to moral law and the account of alienation as the person's refusal of relationship.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: each individual is judged based upon the light
It's a question of do people want a relationship with God

moves.importanceRationale: It is Rauser's fullest direct response to the unfair-belief and coercive-judgment objections.

burdenContact.rationale: It defends the moral character attributed to God in the judgment material.

responseComponents.description: Denies that people are condemned merely for lacking information or a specific belief.
Recasts damnation as freely maintained alienation rather than imposed coercion.

moves.speaker: Aron Ra
moves.claim: Nonbelievers who seek truth but find no evidential basis for religion cannot fairly be described as people who simply reject relationship with God.
moves.warrant: A desire for truth can motivate resistance to unsupported religious claims rather than love of sin or chosen misery.
moves.inference: The alienation account mischaracterizes sincere nonbelief and therefore does not resolve the fairness problem.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This concise reply contrasts the willful-rejection account with truth-seeking nonbelief and states the resulting judgment objection.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: people who want a relationship not necessarily just with God
with whatever is truth
moves.attributionRationale: Aron owns the uninterrupted reply; event 1565 begins a separate misunderstanding that the notes caution against.
moves.importanceRationale: It identifies the central counterexample to treating damnation as purely self-chosen alienation.

burdenContact.rationale: It ties moral responsibility for belief to the evidence accessible to a sincere inquirer.

responseComponents.description: Rejects the inference from nonbelief to refusal of relationship by presenting sincere evidence-based nonbelief.

moves.speaker: Aron Ra
moves.claim: Reasonable belief should be constrained by facts and evidence that can be objectively checked.
moves.warrant: Aron defines evidence as objectively verifiable data that is either positively indicative of or exclusively concordant with one available position over alternatives.
moves.inference: Religious claims should not be accepted as truth unless they can be shown true to the relevant evidential degree.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains Aron's complete linked definitions of fact, evidence, and truth, including the disjunctive evidential standard.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: either positively indicative of or exclusively concordant
the truth is what the facts are
moves.attributionRationale: Aron gives the definitions in one uninterrupted answer.
moves.importanceRationale: This states the con's core standard for what counts as reasonable belief.

burdenContact.rationale: It supplies the test by which the revelatory claim is alleged to lack adequate support.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: A universal requirement of publicly showing a belief true excludes knowledge of one's own private conscious states.
moves.warrant: A person directly experiences a taste or other inner state that another person cannot access, even if testimony or brain activity can be observed.
moves.inference: Objective public verification cannot be a necessary condition for all reasonable knowledge or belief.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This compact passage states the private-state counterexample and its consequence for the verification criterion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: there is something called interior conscious states
I can't show you
moves.attributionRationale: Rauser speaks continuously and supplies a specific licorice example.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly attacks the generality of Aron's evidential rule that governs the motion's reasonableness question.

burdenContact.rationale: It opens conceptual space for reasonable beliefs that are not publicly demonstrable in Aron's sense.

responseComponents.description: Argues that the proposed verification condition is too strong because it excludes ordinary first-person knowledge.

moves.speaker: Aron Ra
moves.claim: Fallible memory does not remove the need for demonstration, but the amount of evidence reasonably demanded should rise with the claim's extremity.
moves.warrant: Aron notes that apparent knowledge can be corrected by later evidence, then treats evidential demand as a sliding scale rather than an absolute certainty requirement.
moves.inference: His standard permits ordinary fallible belief while withholding assent from extraordinary religious claims until proportionate support appears.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The mixed exchange retains Aron's keys-memory example, his Mandela-effect illustration, his explicit sliding-scale qualification, and his application to claims about Jesus; Rauser's short objections provide the live context but are not quoted as Aron's words.

moves.attributionRationale: Rauser interrupts at 1706–1724; Aron's selected premises occur in his clearly separated turns at 1697–1705 and 1725–1765.
moves.importanceRationale: It preserves Aron's qualification that evidential rigor is proportional and compatible with ordinary fallibility.

burdenContact.rationale: It emphasizes error correction as the reason for demonstrability.

responseComponents.description: Replies that private certainty is fallible while clarifying that evidential demands vary with the claim rather than requiring universal certainty.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: The public-verification rule also threatens knowledge of the external world because skeptical scenarios cannot be conclusively shown false.
moves.warrant: Matrix, brain-in-a-vat, Cartesian-demon, and idealist possibilities can fit experience while denying the ordinary external-world picture.
moves.inference: A criterion that yields radical skepticism should be revised rather than used to disqualify religious belief categorically.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is the complete second-stage defeater, from the restated private-state point through the external-world consequence.

moves.importanceRationale: It generalizes the critique of Aron's standard to beliefs Aron himself must retain.

burdenContact.rationale: It supports a fallible rather than certainty-demanding account of reasonable belief.

responseComponents.description: Shows that a universal showing requirement creates skeptical consequences beyond religion.
Distinguishes ordinary fallibility from a criterion that would erase external-world knowledge altogether.

moves.speaker: Aron Ra
moves.claim: By objective verification, Aron means corroboration beyond one person's subjective opinion.
moves.warrant: A claim is objective when others can check it rather than merely receiving the speaker's private assurance.
moves.inference: His evidential rule does not require one particular interlocutor to reproduce every experience, but it does require some independent check.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This short interruption is the complete clarification of what Aron means by 'objective' in response to Rauser's reconstruction of 'I can show you.'

moves.speaker: Aron Ra
moves.claim: Even if ultimate reality were simulated, evidence within the experienced system could still falsify biblical historical claims.
moves.warrant: The stable rules and records of the world as experienced do not support a global flood, regardless of whether the containing reality is fundamental.
moves.inference: Skeptical scenarios do not neutralize ordinary evidence against specific biblical narratives.

moves.claim: The skeptical scenario was offered to test Aron's general epistemic criterion, not to negate evidence about a global flood.

moves.attributionRationale: Rauser speaks continuously and explicitly disclaims the position attributed to him.
moves.importanceRationale: It prevents the epistemic dispute from being misrepresented as a defense of literal flood history.

burdenContact.rationale: It keeps the argument focused on what reasonableness requires rather than on evading particular counterevidence.

moves.speaker: Aron Ra
moves.claim: A nonliteral reading of the flood leaves a problem because Jesus refers to Noah's days as though the event occurred.
moves.warrant: The flood lacks historical support in its biblical form, yet Jesus uses it in teaching without marking it as merely fictional.
moves.inference: Genre flexibility does not fully protect Jesus's reliability or the Bible's revelatory status when a disputed narrative is treated as a historical analogue.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that a later authoritative use of a disputed story complicates the genre defense.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Using Noah or Jonah as a literary analogy does not require either Jesus or the reader to endorse every narrative detail as literal history.
moves.warrant: Jesus invokes Noah to communicate judgment and Jonah to prefigure resurrection, purposes that can operate through a theological story or historical novel.
moves.inference: Those allusions do not establish that Jesus affirmed a global flood or other disputed literalist claims.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage is Rauser's complete answer distinguishing literary appropriation from historical endorsement across the Noah and Jonah examples.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: his point is judgment and he's appropriating and appealing to the story
without requiring the reader to assume
moves.attributionRationale: Rauser speaks continuously in direct response to Aron's Noah-reference challenge.
moves.importanceRationale: It is the direct reply needed to assess whether the Jesus reference defeats genre-sensitive interpretation.

burdenContact.rationale: It shows how Jesus's use of a text can be revelatorily meaningful without literal historical commitment.

responseComponents.description: Distinguishes using a known narrative for judgment imagery from endorsing a global flood as history.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Salvation is reconciliation with God and creation, while Christian accounts need not narrowly require a formulaic profession during this life.
moves.warrant: Rauser distinguishes narrow views from broader inclusivist accounts and cites the sheep-and-goats reversal as a warning against confident in-group and out-group judgments.
moves.inference: The biblical framework can recognize grace beyond visible religious membership and need not condemn sincere nonbelievers as such.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Rauser's complete answer to Aron's request for his personal definition, including the inclusivist warning against group certainty.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: salvation means is being reconciled to God
warn and caution Christians or any religious people
moves.attributionRationale: Rauser answers Aron's request in an uninterrupted turn.
moves.importanceRationale: It supplies the later qualification needed to represent his actual view of salvation and damnation.

burdenContact.rationale: It gives a morally broader reading of biblical salvation that addresses the character objection.

responseComponents.description: Allows that reconciliation and grace may extend beyond explicit religious profession, preserving room for sincere nonbelievers.

moves.speaker: Aron Ra
moves.claim: Divergent Christian accounts of salvation and damnation undermine the clarity and factual grounding expected of revelation.
moves.warrant: Aron contrasts Rauser's account with other Christian accounts, notes that what one side calls damnation may be welcomed by another, and asks why error cannot later be rehabilitated.
moves.inference: Interpretive divergence over ultimate consequences leaves the Bible an unstable guide to the very judgment it announces.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains Aron's complete final challenge from his experience of being labeled through the questions about disparity, clarity, factual basis, and rehabilitation.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: your what you call damnation is my salvation

moves.attributionRationale: Aron speaks continuously until Rauser begins his closing response.
moves.importanceRationale: It adds the distinct clarity and rehabilitation burden after Rauser defines reconciliation inclusively.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that incompatible readings of ultimate judgment count against clear revelation.

responseComponents.description: Challenges whether Rauser's inclusivist definition is textually clear or stable across Christian interpretation.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Reasonable belief and knowledge do not require certainty.
moves.warrant: The possibility of an evil deceiver is a general epistemological issue, and a fallibilist may provisionally trust cognitive processes unless a good defeater is present.
moves.inference: Religious belief can qualify as reasonable without conclusive proof, while remaining open to correction by counterevidence.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The mixed answer contains Rauser's complete move from the deceiver problem to explicit fallibilism; Aron's short agreement that Descartes did not solve the problem and his final agreement with fallibilism are context, not Rauser evidence.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: I don't think that
it is reasonable to accept your beliefs unless you have some good reason not to
moves.attributionRationale: Rauser gives the substantive answer; Aron's brief Descartes agreement at 2541–2542 and final agreement at 2558–2559 are clearly separated and not treated as Rauser's support.
moves.importanceRationale: It states Rauser's affirmative standard for the motion's term 'reasonably believe.'

burdenContact.rationale: It directly defines the epistemic threshold on which the pro position relies.

moves.speaker: Aron Ra
moves.claim: Assuming a mind-independent reality is an unavoidable practical condition of functioning, not an optional faith commitment.
moves.warrant: No person can operate coherently on the denial of that reality, so it is given with ordinary existence rather than freely added as a speculative premise.
moves.inference: Ordinary empirical reasoning has a compulsory shared ground that unsupported supernatural claims do not automatically share.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This audience-answer span contains Aron's full Hume-based response to the charge that objective verification rests on faith in an observer.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: We have no choice but to assume
it is not possible to function on any other assumption
moves.attributionRationale: Aron gives an uninterrupted answer after the moderator reads the question.
moves.importanceRationale: It states the later foundation Aron gives for continuing to trust empirical practice despite skeptical possibilities.

burdenContact.rationale: It distinguishes the baseline needed for inquiry from additional religious commitments requiring evidence.

responseComponents.description: Accepts the inability to escape all skepticism but treats ordinary realism as unavoidable for inquiry.
Explains why the practical evidential framework remains usable even if ultimate certainty is unavailable.

majorLines.omissionRationale: Events 0–369 define worldview, contrast naturalism and supernaturalism, and include extended banter and framing. Their load-bearing moral consequence is retained when Rauser applies worldview revision to objective evil at 370–435; the earlier material does not yet supply a distinct argument about violent revelation.

majorLines.label: Stoning, genocide, and divine perfection
majorLines.omissionRationale: Events 685–712 explain Rauser's steelmanning practice and prior debate/book background; the selected span begins where he actually introduces stoning. Aron's brief Midianite/Canaanite additions and hell challenge remain context inside the retained exchange rather than independent developed moves.

majorLines.label: Biblical diversity, folklore, and governing interpretation
majorLines.omissionRationale: The sequence preserves the anthology analogy, Aron's initial folklore case without importing his later 'some history' clarification into that span, the genre reply, cultural-development challenge, love-centered hermeneutic, and truth/historicity objection. Details about particular religious books are retained only where they carry those selected inferences.

majorLines.label: Jesus's authority, medicine, and historical error
majorLines.omissionRationale: The paired exchange retains Aron's pathogen/demon challenge and Rauser's fallible-benefactor/Ptolemy reply. Events 1267–1395 shift through tone, Christian purpose, Trinity, mediation, and preliminary judgment clarification; the distinct judgment burden begins with Aron's explicit belief-only formulation at 1396.

majorLines.label: Judgment, unforgivable sin, alienation, and sincere nonbelief
majorLines.omissionRationale: All distinct premises in the belief-versus-action, contextual unforgivable-sin, submission/coercion, available-light, chosen-alienation, and sincere-truth-seeker exchange are selected. Events 1565–1604 contain a corrected misunderstanding about whether Rauser denied heaven or hell and illustrative banter; the actual alienation account is already retained.

majorLines.label: Verification, private knowledge, proportional evidence, and skepticism
majorLines.omissionRationale: The selected sequence preserves Aron's disjunctive evidence definition, Rauser's private-state objection, Aron's ordinary-fallibility and sliding-scale qualification, Rauser's external-world defeater, Aron's clarification that objective means independently corroborable, the system-internal evidence reply, and Rauser's criterion-level clarification. Creationist anecdotes and repeated recaps are omitted where they add no independent premise.

majorLines.label: Flood poem, Jesus's Noah reference, and literary allusion
majorLines.omissionRationale: The paired moves retain Aron's concession to metaphorical readings plus his Jesus-reference objection and Rauser's Noah/Jonah literary-allusion response. Events 2064–2099 repeat Aron's broader claim that myths are indefensible before he redirects to judgment, without adding a new premise beyond the selected historicity and judgment lines.

majorLines.label: Final salvation clarification before questions
majorLines.omissionRationale: Events 2100–2221 include repeated requests for Rauser's personal view, narrative restatement, and music/political agreement. The selected moves retain Rauser's actual requested definition and Aron's final disparity, clarity, factual-basis, and rehabilitation challenge. Rauser's closing apology at 2272–2294 is pastoral reflection rather than a new answer to that challenge.

majorLines.label: Audience-question answers
majorLines.omissionRationale: Moderator-read premises are unscored. The selected answers add distinct positions on explicit fallibilism and unavoidable practical realism. Other answers restate intuitive evil, intrinsic wrongness of genocide, love-governed reading, genre study, and nonliteral flood interpretation, or address Satanism, universalism, philosophy, natural theology, and unrelated audience topics without adding a separate motion-level premise.

majorLines.label: Closing remarks and departure
majorLines.omissionRationale: The guests' final remarks concern links, shared interests, mutual agreement on fallibility, and farewell; the substantive fallibilist agreement is already selected from events 2532–2559.

majorLines.omissionRationale: Music, conference promotion, fundraising, channel links, chat greetings, and host announcements occur after both speakers depart and are outside the assessed window.
